scenario.brief:
**Where you are.** `my-notes` is now a repository (Git already knows your name here). The two files are still untracked: Git sees them but has not saved them.

**How saving works.** Saving in Git takes two steps, and that surprises everyone at first:

- First you **stage** a file: you put it in a box of "things to save next". The command is `git add <file>`.
- Then you **commit**: you seal the box with a short message. The command is `git commit -m "your message"`.

The box is called the **staging area**. It exists so you can decide exactly what goes into each save, which becomes useful soon.

**What you'll do.**

1. Stage `notes.md` with `git add notes.md`. Run `git status` afterwards and notice it moved to "Changes to be committed".
2. Commit it with a message, for example `git commit -m "Add my notes file"`.
3. Look at your history with `git log`. One entry, with your name on it.

Leave `todo.md` alone for now. You will save it in the next lab.

**Words you'll meet.** *Stage / staging area*: the box of changes for the next save. *Commit*: one saved point in history, with a message.
scenario.whyItMatters: Commits are the unit of work in every engineering team: code review, releases and bug hunts all happen one commit at a time. Making a small, well-described commit is the most basic professional habit.

steps.content:
# My notes

Things I am learning about Git.

# To do

- Learn what a commit is
- Save my first change

objectives.title: Stage notes.md
objectives.description: git status should list it under "Changes to be committed".
hints: Staging means choosing a file for the next save. The command starts with `git add`.
`git add notes.md` puts that one file in the staging area. `git status` then shows it in green under "Changes to be committed".

objectives.title: Commit it with a message
hints: A commit seals what is staged. It always needs a message that says what you did.
`git commit -m "..."` commits with the message in quotes. Keep it short and clear, like a headline.

objectives.title: Leave todo.md unsaved for now
objectives.description: It should still show as untracked.
hints: Only the files you add are saved. Not adding a file is also a choice.
If you already staged todo.md by mistake, `git restore --staged todo.md` takes it back out of the box.
Run `git status`: notes.md should be gone from the list (it is saved) and todo.md should still be untracked.

debrief.summary: You made your first commit: you chose one file, staged it, and saved it with a message. Git now remembers that version of notes.md forever.
internals: `git add notes.md` copied the file's content into Git's storage and wrote it on the staging list.
`git commit` took everything on the staging list, created a snapshot with your name, the time and your message, and gave it an id (the long string of letters and numbers in `git log`).
todo.md was never on the staging list, so it is not in the snapshot. Git only saves what you add.

keyCommands.note: Choose a file for the next save.
Save what is staged, with a message.
Show the history, newest first. `git log --oneline` is the short form.

commonMistakes: Running `git commit` right after editing and wondering why nothing was saved: the file was never added.
Committing with an empty or vague message like "stuff".
Thinking a commit uploads your work somewhere. It is saved on this computer only; sharing comes in a later track.
debrief.atWork: Engineers stage and commit many times a day. The two-step dance feels odd for a week, then becomes automatic.
debrief.interview: "What is the staging area?" Answer: a holding list between your edited files and a commit, so you decide exactly what each commit contains.
